chunks: The GPU graphics pipeline. The question: What does the GPU pipeline look like?
The graphics pipeline turns a 3D scene made of triangles into the pixels on your screen.

Data flows through stages: first the corner points of the triangles are positioned, then the hardware works out which screen pixels each triangle covers, then each pixel is colored, and finally the nearest surface wins and the result is written to the image.
Some stages run programs, and others are fixed hardware.
Imagine a shadow-puppet stage. A stagehand places cardboard cutouts in the scene (positioning the corners).
A grid of tiny squares on a screen then records which squares each cutout covers (finding the pixels). A painter colors each covered square (coloring).
Finally, if two cutouts overlap on a square, the nearer one hides the farther one. Many cutouts and squares are in progress at the same moment.
One frame as a data flow. The programmable boxes (vertex and fragment shader) run on the same cores. The rest are fixed-function units tuned for throughput.
Each arrow carries a stream, and every box can be busy on a different triangle at the same time.
Vertex: a corner point of a triangle. Rasterization: working out which pixels a triangle covers. Fragment: a candidate pixel produced by a triangle. It may still be hidden.
Shader: a small program run on every vertex or fragment. Depth test: dropping a fragment if something nearer already covers that pixel.
Take one triangle with corners at (0,0), (8,0) and (0,8) on a pixel grid. The vertex stage moves those 3 corners to their screen positions.
The rasterizer then finds that the triangle covers 28 pixel centers (the triangle's area is 32, and the diagonal edge cuts partial pixels).
The fragment shader colors each of the 28 fragments. The depth test then keeps each one only if nothing nearer has already been drawn there.
That is the whole idea: vertices, then pixels, then color, then depth.
"Vertices go through a vertex shader that transforms them to screen space, then primitive assembly builds and clips triangles.

The fixed-function rasterizer finds the pixels each triangle covers, the fragment shader colors them using textures and lighting, and the ROP stage does depth test and blending and writes the framebuffer.
The shaders are programmable and share the same cores, while raster, texture and ROP hardware are fixed-function. Mobile GPUs render by tile to save bandwidth."
